newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's Van Miert warns over BA-American linkup.
newsitem.headline: EU's Van Miert warns over BA-American linkup.

text.p: The European Union sent a new warning to British Airways Plc and American Airlines Tuesday that the EU will not close its eyes to their proposed mega-alliance.

In a speech made available ahead of delivery, EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert repeated earlier statements that the two companies would control 61 percent of the passenger air service between Britain and the United States -- something the European Commission could not ignore.

He also said in the speech to the European Parliament that the commission, the EU's executive body, needed more information on the proposed alliance, despite having already received written and oral answers from both companies to its objections.
Van Miert did not elaborate on the additional information required.

Meanwhile, EU Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock, who shares responsibility with Van Miert for assessing the proposed alliance, said the commission's final decision on the deal will come within weeks, rather than months.
"It's not months, it's not far away...," Kinnock said when asked how long it will take the commission to reach its decision.

The commission's authority to investigate the link-up has been openly challenged by British Airways and the British government. Both argue the British antitrust authorities have a greater say than the commission, whose jurisdiction, they say, applies only to deals involving EU-based carriers.
The Commission points out, however, that the deal would affect U.S. air traffic with mainland Europe, not just Britain.

The commission started separate probes in July into several transatlantic air deals but the link-up between British Airways and American, a unit of AMR Corp., attracted headlines because it is the largest and the commission has publicly said that it raises important competition concerns.

The announcement by Britain's Office of Fair Trading in December that it would clear the alliance on the condition the airlines gave up 168 weekly takeoff and landing "slots" at London's congested London Heathrow airport to make room for rivals did not assuage such fears.
This is because the companies have said, at least publicly, they would sell the slots, not surrender them.
EU legislation provides only for the exchange of slots, as the commission recalled harshly in a letter to the British Department of Industry in January.

The commission sent the two airlines a so-called statement of objections in October detailing its concerns. Van Miert said he had received written and oral answers, but was expecting "supplementary information."
The commission will consult a panel of national experts before reaching a final decision, Van Miert said. He did not say when this would happen.

The alliance also faces a regulatory hurdle in the United States, where it has been made conditional to the conclusion of an "open skies" agreement opening up the UK-U.S. aviation market to competing airlines.
